question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?

question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?

Rule [702.26d] specifies that the phasing event doesn't actually cause a permanent to change zones — a phased-out permanent is just treated as though it doesn't exist while it's phased out, but it never actually left the battlefield zone. Since Banishing Light's exile ability is a one-shot effect tied to the specific event of the enchantment "leaving the battlefield" [610.4], and phasing out doesn't constitute leaving the battlefield, that triggering event simply doesn't occur. This is confirmed directly by the Teferi's Protection ruling: "Any one-shot effects that are waiting 'until [this] leaves the battlefield,' such as that of Banishing Light, won't happen when a permanent phases out."

So when your Banishing Light phases out (along with your other permanents) due to Teferi's Protection, the exiled creature stays exiled. Banishing Light will phase back in during your next untap step (as described by Teferi's Protection's own reminder text and rule [702.26c]), still exiled the same creature under the same continuous effect, since nothing happened to end that effect. The creature would only return if Banishing Light actually leaves the battlefield for real (e.g., is destroyed or sacrificed) — phasing in and out doesn't count as such an event, and no zone-change triggers fire from phasing [702.26d].

This applies the same way in a multiplayer or Commander game — phasing still isn't a zone change regardless of how many players are involved, so the exile effect is unaffected by phasing in any game size.

question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
reference:

Why targeting is legal: When you cast Emrakul, the physical card is put on the stack as a spell [405.1], and its 'When you cast this spell...' ability triggers at that time and is put on the stack as a separate triggered ability (with no card associated with it) the next time a player would receive priority [603.1a][405.1][117.2a]. Your opponent then casts Counterspell 'in response to' that trigger, meaning Counterspell goes on the stack above it and will resolve first [In Response To][117.7]. Counterspell's text 'Counter target spell' targets the spell Emrakul on the stack, not a permanent, per the rule that a description referring to a card type without specifying a zone/word 'card' etc. normally means a permanent, but a description using the word 'spell' means an object on the stack [109.2b]. Emrakul's protection from instants only functions while Emrakul is on the battlefield as a static/protection ability of a permanent; per the Emrakul rulings, 'Protection abilities only apply while the object with the ability is on the battlefield. Notably, Emrakul may be the target of a spell that targets it while on the stack, such as Syncopate.' Since Emrakul is a spell on the stack (not yet a permanent), it has no protection there, so Counterspell's targeting is legal [115.1a] (the only targeting restriction relevant here, that a spell/ability can't target itself, doesn't apply since Counterspell and Emrakul are different objects [115.5]).

What happens if Counterspell resolves: Counterspell will resolve before Emrakul, since it was cast in response and resolves first [117.7][608.2m]. It counters the Emrakul spell, meaning Emrakul is countered and never resolves as a permanent. However, the separate triggered ability 'When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent...' is already on the stack below Counterspell and is unaffected by Emrakul being countered — per the Emrakul ruling, 'An ability that triggers when a player casts a spell resolves before the spell that caused it to trigger. It resolves even if that spell is countered or otherwise leaves the stack without resolving.' So that triggered ability will still resolve on its own turn on the stack, granting you control of the targeted opponent during that opponent's next turn, and after that turn the opponent still takes an extra turn, exactly as described in the Emrakul rulings.

Note also that activated/triggered abilities and spells are countered by different kinds of effects: Counterspell only counters spells [113.9], so it can counter the Emrakul spell but could never have countered the triggered ability itself even if targeted at it (which it isn't here, since Counterspell only targets spells).

question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
reference:
Yes, the cascade trigger is satisfied, but whether you can cast the Tibalt side for free depends on your cascade spell's mana value.

Cascade works as follows: “When you cast this spell, exile cards from the top of your library until you exile a nonland card whose mana value is less than this spell's mana value. You may cast that card without paying its mana cost if the resulting spell's mana value is less than this spell's mana value.” [702.85a]

Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a modal double-faced card (MDFC), not a transforming DFC. Per the card's rulings, the mana value of an MDFC depends on which zone/state it's in: while it sits in the exile zone (i.e., before you decide to cast it), only the front face's mana value is used — that's Valki's mana value 2. So for the purpose of stopping the cascade exile process, the card is treated as MV 2. As long as your cascade spell's mana value is greater than 2, exiling Valki // Tibalt is a legal stopping point for the cascade trigger.

Now, when you choose to actually cast the exiled card, MDFC rules let you pick which face to cast (front or back), just as with a normal cast — casting a double-faced spell defaults to the front face unless something lets you cast the back face, and for a genuinely modal DFC that "something" is simply the normal choice you make whenever you cast the card [712.11c][712.11d]. If you choose to cast the back face (Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor), the resulting spell on the stack is evaluated using that face's own characteristics — per the card's ruling, on the stack an MDFC's mana value is based on whichever face is face up. Tibalt's front-face-printed mana cost is {5}{B}{R}, giving Tibalt a mana value of 7 as the spell that would go on the stack.

Cascade only lets you cast the exiled card for free "if the resulting spell's mana value is less than this spell's mana value" [702.85a]. So:
- The cascade hit itself is legal as long as your cascade spell's mana value is greater than 2 (Valki's front-face mana value, used while the card sits in exile).
- You may cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face for free only if your cascade spell's mana value is greater than 7 (Tibalt's mana value as the face-up spell). If your cascade spell's mana value is 7 or less, you cannot legally cast the Tibalt side off the cascade trigger — you could still choose to cast the Valki side for free instead (since its resulting mana value, 2, will satisfy the "less than" requirement for essentially any cascade spell with MV 3 or higher), or simply decline to cast the exiled card, sending it to the bottom of your library along with any other exiled-but-uncast cards.
